It presents a portfolio overview, corporate overview, strategic review, ESG overview, statutory reports, and financial statements. It details five safety incidents with fatalities, including a tanker driver fall, a workman slipping from pipes, an RTG container collision, an electric shock from an overhead line, and a piling tripod collapse. Actions taken to strengthen safety are listed for each incident. It also provides fatality data by year (FY21-FY25), lost time injury (LTI) details, lost time injury frequency rate (LTIFR) details, and total person-hours worked for employees and contractors in FY 2024-25.

structure.title: Building strong ties with communities
structure.summary: The section outlines the organization's commitment to community prosperity through its 'Growth with Goodness' philosophy, detailing CSR strategy, focus areas (education, climate action, health, livelihoods, community development), and alignment with SDGs and regulatory compliance. It presents CSR expenditure and beneficiary data, including women and specially-abled individuals. The community engagement approach covers stakeholder policy, impact assessments, grievance mechanisms, transparency, and support for vulnerable groups. Education initiatives include Adani Foundation's schools, Project Utthan, Udaan exposure tours, and specific school profiles, highlighting student outcomes and improvements in learning, literacy, and confidence.

nodes.title: Community Engagement and CSR Strategy Overview
nodes.summary: The page outlines the organization's commitment to community prosperity through empowerment and sustainable development, guided by the 'Growth with Goodness' philosophy. It details key linkages including capital impacted, SDGs aligned, material topics, key risks and opportunities, and GRI linkage. CSR focus areas covered are education, climate action, health and nutrition, sustainable livelihoods, and community development. It presents the CSR vision and mission statements, emphasizing social obligations and facilitation of development without discrimination. The CSR approach describes the Adani Foundation's strategic initiatives since 1996, aligned with national priorities and SDGs, spanning 6,769 villages across 19 states and impacting 9.1 million lives. Regulatory compliance references are also included.

Supporting vulnerable communities through Adani Foundation includes women's empowerment (CHETNA, menstrual hygiene, Pink Toilet) and integration of specially-abled persons.

structure.summary: This text from Adani Ports and SEZ's Integrated Annual Report 2024-25 covers the Adani Foundation's healthcare and nutrition initiatives. It addresses India's non-communicable disease burden and rural maternal/child mortality through Mobile Healthcare Units (MHCUs) for primary care, rural clinics and hospitals for secondary/tertiary care, and Project SuPoshan for malnutrition and anaemia. It details MHCU services, health camps, 7 rural clinics and 1 wellness centre serving 40,325 patients, and 1,10,670 treatments. It highlights GAIMS Bhuj (43,643 OPD, 3.95+ lakh IPD), a burn care centre, the Adani Vision Care Program (1,16,867 screened, 36,319 eyeglasses), Adani Hospital Mundra (47,376 OPD, 2,616 IPD), and the Village Sanitation Programme in Krishnapatnam benefiting 18,000 families across 8 villages with 136 community workers.

structure.title: Sustainable livelihoods
structure.summary: The Adani Foundation's Integrated Annual Report 2024-25 section on sustainable livelihoods covers its initiatives to improve community livelihoods through a self-sustaining ecosystem. It details programs across on-farm, off-farm, and non-farm sectors, including natural farming, irrigation, animal husbandry, dairy development, and women-owned enterprises. The report highlights women empowerment through Self-Help Groups (SHGs) with specific turnover figures from Mundra, Hazira, Dahej, Dhamra, and Vizhinjam, and the CHETNA initiative promoting gender diversity. It also covers menstrual hygiene awareness, agriculture programs with yield improvements and farmer benefits, and animal husbandry efforts including fodder support, vaccination, dairy development, and veterinary services.

structure.title: Project Swavlamban (Mundra)
structure.summary: Project Swavlamban in Mundra provides technical kits to divyang students and launches a book. The Adani Foundation's CSR initiatives include village infrastructure (community sheds, halls, fitness centers, RO water units, streetlights, playgrounds), fisherfolk empowerment (education kits, transportation, scholarships, job placements, potable water), skill development (ASDC courses, government scheme facilitation, electric vehicle support for disabled), climate action (water conservation, mangrove plantation, afforestation, Green School Initiative, coastal cleanup), renewable energy (solar installations), disaster relief (floods in Andhra Pradesh, Wayanad landslide), and grievance redressal with 95% resolution. Value creation stories highlight Raysi's journey and women's drudgery reduction. Responsible procurement objectives and commitments are also covered.

structure.title: Key Highlights
key_items: Key Supplier ESG Programme Features; ENVIRONMENT
structure.summary: This text from Adani Ports and SEZ's Integrated Annual Report 2024-25 covers supply chain management, including supplier metrics (6,442 total suppliers, 206 Tier 1 significant suppliers, 71% spend on significant Tier 1 suppliers, 78% local procurement from India, 56% from same state, 22% from same district). It details supplier screening aspects (environmental, social, governance, business relevance) and risk screening methodology (sustainability risk matrix, country/sector/commodity risks). It outlines the Supplier Code of Conduct and Sustainable Procurement Policy, covering human rights, risk management, safety, ethics, GHG reduction, fair employment, governance, environmental impact, and due diligence. Key supply chain elements include supplier assessment, onboarding, training, monitoring, and communication. The Supplier ESG Programme features minimum ESG requirements, exclusion of non-compliant suppliers, preference for superior ESG profiles, training, board oversight, and continuous review. It describes supplier screening criteria, a grading system (O, B, A grades based on annual revenue), supplier oversight (scoring system, annual reviews, extended evaluations), and screening of significant suppliers using ESG considerations and a sustainability risk matrix. It also covers pre-qualification and risk assessment, onboarding, preliminary audits (desk-based/on-site assessments, third-party audits), with 100% of new suppliers screened using environmental and social criteria, and 100% of significant suppliers assessed.

structure.title: Risk Assessment and Due Diligence
structure.summary: The text covers APSEZ's supplier ESG risk assessment and due diligence, including country, sector, and commodity-specific risks, an integrated scorecard requiring a minimum score of 90, and metrics on suppliers assessed, corrective actions, and terminations. It details corrective action and continuous improvement processes, mitigation plans, and periodic re-assessments. Supplier development initiatives are described: Suraksha Samvad for safety culture, Sampark for shared vision, Saksham for skill empowerment with 44,770 trained, ESG awareness sessions for 241 suppliers, and a supplier engagement survey. The governance section outlines a robust framework with a one-tier board, key highlights (board size 10, 10% women, zero cybersecurity incidents), core values (courage, trust, commitment), material topics, GRI linkages, and capitals impacted.

structure.title: Our Corporate Governance Structure
structure.summary: The text covers APSEZ's corporate governance structure, detailing the Board of Directors' role and its specialized committees: Audit, Corporate Responsibility, Risk Management, Nomination and Remuneration, Corporate Social Responsibility, Mergers & Acquisitions, Reputation Risk, Stakeholders' Relationship, Information Technology & Data Security, and Legal, Regulatory & Tax. It also provides Board composition and structure metrics, including the number of executive, non-executive, and independent directors, board diversity, meeting attendance, compensation ratio, and committee meetings, along with a governance hierarchy from Board-level committees to site-level sustainability committees.

structure.title: Approach to Corporate Governance
structure.summary: This section details APSEZ's corporate governance approach, covering the Code of Business Ethics and policies, systems and SOPs for responsible conduct including anti-bribery, whistleblower policies, and compliance systems like Legatrix. It outlines the grievance management system and reports zero ethical breaches. Board accountability is highlighted with attendance, performance evaluations, and familiarisation programmes. The section extensively covers technology initiatives: Navis TOS, IPOS, logistics tracking, customer portals, Vizhinjam Port automation, and digital transformation roadmap. It discusses automation benefits, customer satisfaction surveys and ESG focus, and cybersecurity governance, including consequence management, business continuity planning, and specific cybersecurity initiatives. Data privacy governance and protection practices under the DPDP Act are detailed, along with personal information protection and independent assurance statements on sustainability reporting.

It reports zero breaches in eight ethical categories for FY 2024-25. The document also covers Board accountability, noting over 75% meeting attendance, shareholder approval for MoA/AoA changes, and D&O insurance. Board performance evaluation includes internal self-assessment via the Nomination and Remuneration Committee and an external review by Talentonic HR Solutions, with findings leading to improvement initiatives.

nodes.title: Board Familiarisation Programme
nodes.summary: The text covers APSEZ's Board Familiarisation Programme, including induction, ongoing education, risk management, and annual assessment. It details the Board election process and strict independence criteria for Independent Directors. It describes advocacy and leadership efforts, including policy engagement, a governance framework for policy advocacy, and a framework for addressing misalignments with trade associations. It lists industry associations and principles subscriptions. It also covers digitalisation and cybersecurity, highlighting technology investments, digital transformation initiatives, employee digital literacy, and specific technologies like IoT, RFID, algorithmic optimisation, 3D scanning, video analytics, Command & Control, and Port Community System to enhance operational efficiency and cybersecurity.

nodes.title: Navis Terminal Operating System – Efficiently manages port operations by:
nodes.summary: The text covers Navis TOS for vessel, yard, and route planning with real-time cargo visibility; IPOS for port transactions, marine/vessel/gate operations, documentation, resource allocation, and monitoring across dry, bulk, break bulk, ODC, and liquid cargo. First/last-mile visibility includes FarEye for multimodal tracking and exception management, FOIS for freight train tracking and rake optimization, LMS for logistics close-looping, and FleetX for fleet safety, geofencing, and pilferage detection. Terminal cargo management uses Tracker for container tracking, yard/gate optimization, and GPS integration, and CMS for booking, inventory, and revenue management. Customer interactions via Adani Customer Portal. Vizhinjam Port automation features semi-automated RMQCs, automated CRMGs, OCR gates, RFID, and RTLS/MLT-equipped ITVs, yielding efficiency and transshipment gains. Other initiatives include zero-touch customer experience at Virochannagar MMLP, proprietary interaction portal, Ahmedabad Strategic Command Centre for centralized monitoring and analytics, in-house TMS marketplace, and a 2023-2028 digital roadmap (Navis, PCS, central C&C, digital twin, AI/ML, automation, AGV, zero-touch ITUP). Case study details command centre benefits and track-and-trace risk assessment with GPS, RFID, QR, ANPR, biometrics, and PCS/government integration.

It also covers APSEZ's major tech initiatives: hinterland connectivity integration via a zero-touch customer programme at Virochannagar MMLP and a proprietary interaction portal; a state-of-the-art Strategic Command Centre in Ahmedabad for real-time tracking, data analytics, SLA monitoring, and interlinked local command centres; and an in-house Trucking Management Solution (TMS) marketplace with real-time tracking and customer system integration.

nodes.title: Key Automation Benefits
nodes.summary: The text outlines automation benefits in port operations, including reduced manual handling, increased cargo throughput, and enhanced safety, positioning India in the global supply chain. It details APSEZ's digital transformation roadmap from FY 2023-24 to FY 2027-28, covering phases like NextGen foundation, scaling digitalisation, transformation, reimagination, and smart operations. It highlights the Strategic Command Centre, Track & Trace technologies, and various technological innovations such as auto-steering for RTGs, robotic e-RTGs, and container position detection. Customer satisfaction initiatives, including surveys and a customer value proposition model, are described, along with ESG compliance and a satisfaction score trend from FY 2021-22 to FY 2024-25.

nodes.title: Technology-Driven Customer Satisfaction and ESG Survey at APSEZ
nodes.summary: The page covers APSEZ's use of technology to enhance customer satisfaction, including IT systems for cargo and vessel status, auto-steering for RTGs, remotely operated robotic e-RTGs, dredger modification, container position detection, and handling complex cargo. It highlights innovations like a floating Ro-Ro terminal, largest dredging capability, berthing aid system, hydrocarbon detectors, and zero vessel waste. It also details the customer value proposition model with a diverse customer base, differentiated end-to-end solutions, and long-term relationship nurturing via smart port initiatives. Finally, it describes customer satisfaction surveys, their ESG focus, and key survey topics and findings.

nodes.title: Customer Satisfaction Survey Results
nodes.summary: The text presents customer satisfaction survey results for FY 2021-22 to FY 2024-25, showing scores out of 5 (4.1, 4.3, 4.5, 4.3), percentage of satisfied customers (82, 86, 90, 86), and 100% coverage. It then details APSEZ's focus on cybersecurity, including its governance framework with a Board-level IT & Data Security Committee, Chief Digital Officer, and Head Cyber Security. The committee's responsibilities are outlined, along with the cyber risk management strategy aligned with ISO 27001, cybersecurity infrastructure (24/7 Cyber Defence Centre, ISMS), audit and compliance practices, and incident management and response protocols, including bi-annual testing, escalation processes, and grievance management.

nodes.title: Consequence Management for Non-compliance
nodes.summary: APSEZ follows a robust consequence management protocol for cybersecurity non-compliance, including data leak protection agents on all devices, outbound communication scrutiny, breach identification by the Information Protection Group, escalation of unresolved incidents to senior leadership, and invocation of the IT Consequence Management Policy by HR for appropriate actions. Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions monitor and isolate compromised systems in real time, with SIEM integrated for threat correlation and analysis. The Business Continuity Plan ensures uninterrupted operations during natural disasters, cyber threats, and other disruptions affecting Port and SEZ operations, addressing personnel, facilities, and technology compromises that impact essential IT services.

nodes.title: The BCP Framework
nodes.summary: The text outlines APSEZ's Business Continuity Plan (BCP) framework, detailing crisis management structure, activation protocols, core elements, and semi-annual testing. It covers oversight by the CISO, cybersecurity measures, annual training for employees (3,212 trained in FY 2024-25), and operational improvements including GMS, ITUP, Commvault AirGap, and GOS. It lists various cybersecurity initiatives such as PAM, SOAR, CSPM, MFA, WAF, SIEM, EDR, DLP, deep/dark web monitoring, proxy, NAC, and IAM, describing their purposes and impacts in enhancing security, incident response, and compliance. The overall aim is resilience, security, and uninterrupted service.

nodes.title: APSEZ Business Continuity, Cybersecurity, and Operational Resilience Initiatives
nodes.summary: The page covers APSEZ's Business Continuity Plan (BCP) activation, including its purpose, phases, resources, and semi-annual testing. It details oversight by the CISO, cybersecurity awareness training for 3,212 employees, and operational improvements through systems like GMS, ITUP, Commvault AirGap, and GOS. It also lists cybersecurity initiatives such as PAM, SOAR, CSPM, MFA, WAF, SIEM, EDR, DLP, deep/dark web monitoring, and proxy/NAC, each with purpose and impact. The overall focus is on maintaining resilience, security, and uninterrupted service through comprehensive BCP, cybersecurity measures, and continuous operational enhancements.

nodes.title: Identity and Access Management
nodes.summary: The text covers Identity and Access Management initiatives including website security, HTTP traffic filtering, grievance collection, ransomware protection, gate automation, SIEM, endpoint monitoring, data loss prevention, web monitoring, proxy servers, NAC, and digital identity management, with their purposes. It details data privacy governance, a comprehensive Data Privacy Policy, PII protection, privacy risk assessment aligned with DPDP Act, detection mechanisms (IDS, DLP, SIEM, access logs, incident reporting), reporting procedures, privacy impact assessments (PIA) steps, and data protection practices like secure storage, controlled sharing, consent, deletion, anonymization, purpose-specific usage, regulatory compliance, privacy by design, and personal information protection. It also notes the B2B context and absence of opt-out necessity.

nodes.title: APSEZ Data Privacy Governance and Protection Practices
nodes.summary: APSEZ prioritizes data protection as a core value, formulating a comprehensive Data Privacy Policy covering all stakeholders, with the Head - Cybersecurity responsible for compliance. The framework aligns with the DPDP Act and includes detection mechanisms (IDS, DLP, SIEM, access logs, incident reporting), reporting procedures (internal, regulatory, stakeholder notification), and Privacy Impact Assessments (PIA) with key steps. Data protection practices include safe storage (5-7 years), controlled information sharing via SharePoint with approvals, seeking consent, data deletion, anonymisation, purpose-specific usage, regulatory compliance for disclosures, and Privacy by Design principles (data minimisation, encryption, role-based access).

nodes.title: Protection of Personal Information
nodes.summary: This section covers APSEZ's personal data protection under the DPDP Act 2023, including authorization, encryption, audits, training, incident response, a zero-tolerance policy, no reported breaches or fines for three years, and grievance channels. It includes TUV India's independent assurance statement on APSEZL's Sustainability Report, detailing management responsibility, scope, verification methodology, onsite verification, responsibilities, improvement opportunities, and conclusion on ESG disclosures. It lists GRI indicators 16–30, defines reporting boundaries, and describes a risk-based verification approach. The conclusion confirms fair representation across all six capitals and adherence to AA1000 principles. It outlines intellectual, human, social, and natural capital, reporting quality principles, and TUVI's independence. Finally, it includes a certification statement and lists the board of directors, their profiles, board committees, and global tax contributions.

nodes.title: Protection of Personal Information (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers APSEZ's personal data protection measures under the DPDP Act 2023, including authorization, encryption, audits, training, and incident response. It notes a zero-tolerance policy, no reported breaches or fines for three years, and ongoing development of grievance channels. Training topics and effectiveness measurement are detailed. The document also includes an independent assurance statement by TUV India on APSEZL's Sustainability Report, covering management responsibility, scope, verification methodology, opportunities for improvement, and conclusion on ESG disclosures.

structure.summary: The text outlines APSEZ's responsible tax practices, emphasizing full compliance, transparency, and governance. It details the tax governance structure, including board oversight and risk management, and lists principles like compliance, transparency, governance, and stakeholder engagement. It reports global tax contributions of ₹10,438 crore for FY 2024-25, broken down by direct, indirect, and other categories, with country-wise and state-wise breakdowns. It highlights customs contributions, assurance by consultants, and provides corporate information such as board members, committees, auditors, and bankers, along with a shareholder communication regarding green initiatives.

structure.summary: This annexure to the Directors' Report details energy conservation, technology absorption, and foreign exchange earnings/outgo under Section 134(3)(m) of the Companies Act, 2013. It covers steps taken for energy conservation (solar usage, LED replacements, efficient ACs, pumps, open access renewable energy), capital investments in energy conservation equipment (including electric heavy equipment), technology absorption efforts (LED conversion, smart meters, electromagnetic water meters, safety systems like Twin Twenty Detection, auto lubrication, dust suppression, AI human detection), benefits derived (cost savings), imported technology (crane OCR systems, electric equipment), R&D expenditure (not applicable), and foreign exchange earnings and outgo for 2023-24 and 2024-25.

structure.title: Annexure to the Directors’ Report

It details the CSR Committee's composition, including changes in membership, and provides a web-link to disclosures. Financial details include average net profit of ₹198.18 crore, 2% obligation of ₹3.97 crore, and total CSR spend of ₹4.47 crore (projects: ₹4.38 crore, overheads: ₹0.09 crore), with an excess of ₹0.50 crore available for set-off. No impact assessment was applicable. The report confirms no unspent amounts for the past three years, no capital assets created, and no failure to spend the required 2%. It is signed by the Chairman and CSR Committee Chairman.

structure.title: Management Discussion & Analysis

It focuses on India's economic outlook, highlighting GDP growth projections, GST growth, RBI rate cuts, inflation trends, and India's economic position and targets. The section then discusses global maritime trade trends, India's EXIM trade, port sector overview, policy developments, and logistics industry growth. It presents APSEZ's business overview, including ports, logistics, SEZ, marine services, global expansion, sustainability goals, and FY 2024-25 performance. Operational growth, capacity targets, sustainability efforts, ESG highlights, business strategy, risk management, HR initiatives, internal controls, and a cautionary statement on forward-looking statements are also covered.

nodes.title: Outlook
nodes.summary: The text provides a global economic overview covering resilience amid geopolitical tensions and cost-of-living crises, with IMF growth at 3.3% for 2024 and infrastructure market at USD 3.05 billion. It details advanced economies (US GDP 2.8%, Euro area 0.9%) and emerging markets (China 5.0%, overall 4.3%). Inflation trends, central bank policies, oil and coal prices, and outlook to 2026 are discussed. It then focuses on India as a fast-growing economy, highlighting GDP slowdown to 6.5% in FY 2024-25, GST growth, RBI's rate cuts to 6.0%, declining CPI and WPI inflation, and India's position as fifth-largest economy with targets for 2027-28 and 2047, including capital investment budget.

nodes.title: Outlook
nodes.summary: The text provides a comprehensive outlook on India's economy, projecting 6.2% GDP growth in 2025 driven by infrastructure, capex, and reforms, with details on demographic dividend, inflation, RBI policy, and government schemes. It then covers global maritime trade trends, challenges, and policy implications. India's EXIM trade, port sector overview (major and non-major ports, cargo volumes, top ports like Mundra, policy developments like Sagarmala, National Ports Bill, etc.), and logistics industry growth (market size, trends, digital transformation, sustainability) are discussed. APSEZ's business overview, including its ports, logistics, SEZ, marine services, global expansion, sustainability goals, and FY 2024-25 performance highlights and financial ratios, is presented.

nodes.title: Outlook
nodes.summary: The text covers APSEZ's operational growth, including 450 MMT cargo volume and 7% growth, Mundra Port's 200 MMT milestone, logistics expansion, domestic and international acquisitions and operations. Future capacity targets and infrastructure developments are outlined. Sustainability efforts include electrification, renewable energy, and mangrove afforestation. ESG highlights detail carbon neutrality goals, investments, and initiatives. Business strategy focuses on ESG leadership, customer-centricity, national and global expansion, diversification, operational excellence, and partnerships. Risk management framework and mitigation strategies are described, along with HR initiatives, employee engagement, and recognition. Internal control systems and audit processes are summarized, followed by a cautionary statement on forward-looking statements.

It specifically covers Dr. Ravindra Dholakia's roles in various committees for FY 2024-25, including the Audit Committee, Nomination and Remuneration Committee, Stakeholders' Relationship Committee, Compliance Officer, investor complaints, Corporate Social Responsibility Committee, Risk Management Committee, and non-statutory committees, along with meeting frequencies, attendance, and compositional changes.

nodes.title: Board of Directors
nodes.summary:
Board of Directors
The Board is the highest authority for the governance and the custodian who push our business in the right direction and is responsible for the establishment of cultural, ethical, sustainable and accountable growth of the Company. The Board is constituted with a high level of integrated, knowledgeable and committed professionals. The Board provides strategic guidance and independent views to the Company’s senior management while discharging its fiduciary responsibilities. The Board also provides direction and exercises appropriate control to ensure that the Company is managed in a manner that fulfils stakeholders’ aspirations and societal expectations.

nodes.title: Size and Composition
nodes.summary: The text details the Board's size and composition, emphasizing diversity and compliance with the Companies Act, 2013, SEBI Listing Regulations, and other statutory provisions. As of March 31, 2025, the Board has ten directors: three executive directors (30%), two non-executive non-independent directors (20%), and five non-executive independent directors (50%), including one woman. It provides director names, categories, and percentages, and includes visual breakdowns of board composition by director type and gender (90% men, 10% women). It notes the Board's professionalism and competence, and clarifies that no directors are related except Gautam S. Adani and Rajesh S. Adani (brothers) and Karan Adani (son of Gautam S. Adani).

Adani, Karan Adani, Ashwani Gupta, P. S. Jayakumar, Bharat Sheth, Ravindra Dholakia, P. K. Pujari, M. V. Bhanumathi, and Rajkumar Beniwal. It also includes the Board's age profile and experience distribution, a list of core skills and competencies, and a table highlighting the specific areas of expertise of each director.

nodes.title: Directors’ selection, appointment and tenure:
nodes.summary: The text outlines directors' selection, appointment, and tenure: directors are appointed by the Board on the Nomination and Remuneration Committee's recommendation and shareholder approval; all except Executive Chairman and Independent Directors retire by rotation; Executive Directors serve per the Act and employment terms. For Independent Directors, the policy aligns with the Act and SEBI Listing Regulations, with a five-year term subject to shareholder approval. It notes no Independent Director resigned early, and compliance with SEBI Regulations limiting directorships to seven listed companies and committee memberships to ten (and chairpersons to five). All directors disclosed committee positions. Finally, the company provides Directors' and Officers' Liability Insurance covering directors, officers, and employees acting in managerial or supervisory capacities, including those serving subsidiaries/joint ventures/associates at the company's request.

nodes.title: Independent Directors
nodes.summary: The text covers Independent Directors' compliance with SEBI Listing Regulations and the Companies Act, including confirmations of independence, databank enrollment, and formal appointment letters. It details Board changes: appointments of Dr. Ravindra Dholakia and Mr. P. K. Pujari, re-appointment of Mr. P. S. Jayakumar, and cessation of Mr. G. K. Pillai and Prof. G. Raghuram. It outlines Board meeting procedures, including scheduling, agenda preparation, information access, and the minimum four pre-scheduled meetings per year, along with additional meetings and resolutions by circulation.

nodes.title: Board Composition, Changes, Meetings, and Procedures
nodes.summary: The text covers independent directors' compliance, appointment letters, and website link. It details board changes: appointments of Dr. Dholakia and Mr. Pujari, re-appointment of Mr. Jayakumar, and cessation of Mr. Pillai and Prof. Raghuram. It describes board meeting procedures: schedule finalized with members, advance communication, board calendar on website, additional meetings for urgent matters, unanimous acceptance of committee recommendations, board focus on strategic issues and risk management, and attendance of CFO, senior management, and functional heads at meetings.

nodes.title: Availability of information to the Board
nodes.summary: The Board has full access to Company information, Senior Management, and auditors. Meetings follow a structured agenda with comprehensive background information circulated in advance; supplementary items and table agendas are allowed for urgent matters. At least four pre-scheduled meetings are held annually, with additional meetings and resolutions by circulation as needed. Detailed presentations cover financials, operations, strategy, and risks. Compliance reports are reviewed regularly, and Board decisions are communicated with action taken reports at subsequent meetings. During the year, four Board meetings were held on specified dates, with required quorum. Attendance details for directors at Board meetings and the AGM are provided, including changes in directorship. The Board accepted all statutory Committee recommendations, ensuring compliance with SEBI Listing Regulations.

nodes.title: Meeting of Independent Directors
nodes.summary:
Meeting of Independent Directors
The Independent Directors meet at least once in a year, without the presence of Executive Directors or Management representatives. They also have separate meeting(s) with the Chairman of the Board, to discuss issues and concerns, if any. The Independent Directors met once during the Financial Year 2024-25, on March 29, 2025. The Independent Directors inter alia discuss the issues arising out of the Committee Meetings and Board discussion including the quality, quantity and timely flow of information between the Company Management and the Board that is necessary for the Board to effectively and reasonably perform its duties. In addition to these formal meetings, interactions outside the Board Meetings also take place between the Chairman and Independent Directors.
Statutory Auditors also have independent access to the members of the Audit Committee to discuss internal audit effectiveness, control environment and their general feedback. The Independent Directors also have access to Secretarial Auditor and the management for discussions and questions, if any.

nodes.title: Directors’ Induction and Familiarisation
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Board Familiarization Program for new directors, including induction covering company history, culture, structure, and businesses; immersion sessions by senior executives on industry trends, operations, growth strategy, and ESG; and strategy sessions. It details the Directors’ Engagement Series, which apprises the Board on topics like ESG, capital markets, risk management, and digital initiatives, with four events held featuring multiple sessions and site visits. Additionally, an annual strategy meet allows the Board to discuss strategic planning, risks, and new programs, providing comprehensive perspectives and interaction with senior leadership.

nodes.title: Remuneration Policy:
nodes.summary: The Remuneration Policy focuses on rewarding performance, attracting and retaining executives, and ensuring optimal director remuneration. It details non-executive director remuneration via commission (up to 1% of net profits for 5 years from April 1, 2020, and a new approval for 5 years from April 1, 2025, subject to member approval), sitting fees (₹75,000 for board/audit, ₹35,000 for other committees), and expense reimbursement. It covers D&O liability insurance, performance evaluation criteria for independent directors, and executive director remuneration including fixed pay, variable pay linked to financial and ESG metrics. It also provides remuneration details for non-executive and executive directors for FY 2024-25, shareholding of directors, and notes no stock options or severance fees.

nodes.title: Details of Remuneration:
nodes.summary: The text details remuneration for Non-Executive Directors (sitting fees and commission, including participation fees, with notes on directors who ceased or were appointed during the year) and Executive Directors (salary, perquisites, allowances, other benefits, and commission, with notes on payables in FY 2025-26), states no other pecuniary relationships or stock options for Non-Executive Directors, lists shares held by Directors as of March 31, 2025 (including specific share counts and a trust holding), and notes no Employees' Stock Option Scheme or severance fees.

nodes.title: Board Committees
nodes.summary:
Board Committees
The Board Committees play a vital role in ensuring sound Corporate Governance practices. The Committees are constituted to handle specific activities and ensure speedy resolution of the diverse matters. nodes.title: a) Current versus non-current classification
nodes.summary: The text outlines the basis of preparation and material accounting policies for standalone financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2025. nodes.title: c) Fair value measurement
nodes.summary: This note outlines the Company's fair value measurement accounting policy, covering measurement of financial instruments at each balance sheet date, definition of fair value based on principal or advantageous market, market participant assumptions, highest and best use for non-financial assets, and valuation techniques maximizing observable inputs. nodes.title: d) Revenue recognition
nodes.summary: The text covers revenue recognition policies: general criteria for contracts with customers, specific rules for port operation services (including multiple obligations, variable consideration, take-or-pay charges), license fees/waterfront royalty, infrastructure premium, interest income using effective interest rate, and dividends. It also addresses government grants recognition (expense-related and asset-related, including concessional waterfront royalty), exceptional items disclosure, and taxes (current income tax including MAT, measurement, and recognition outside profit or loss).

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition, Government Grants, and Exceptional Items Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: Revenue recognition for license fees, waterfront royalty, revenue share, infrastructure premium, interest income using effective interest rate, and dividends. Government grants recognized with reasonable assurance, with expense-related grants as income over matching periods and asset-related grants as income over useful life or deducted from asset carrying amount. Waterfront royalty under concession agreement paid at concessional rates per Gujarat Maritime Board notification. Exceptional items disclosed separately when size, type, or incidence requires disclosure to improve understanding of performance.

nodes.title: g) Taxes
nodes.summary: The section covers income tax accounting policies for current tax (including MAT and uncertain positions) and deferred tax (recognition, measurement, exceptions, review, and MAT credit). It details right-of-use assets and lease liabilities, short-term/low-value lease exemptions, lessor accounting, inventory valuation, impairment of non-financial assets, provisions and contingencies, and employee benefits. Financial instruments are covered extensively: initial recognition and measurement, subsequent measurement categories (amortised cost, FVTPL, FVTOCI for debt and equity), perpetual debt, derecognition, impairment using the ECL model, financial liabilities, loans and borrowings, financial guarantee contracts, offsetting, derivatives, redeemable preference shares, cash and cash equivalents, dividends, and earnings per share. Business combinations, new standards adopted, and significant judgements (de facto control) and estimates (impairment, taxes, fair value, depreciation) are also addressed, along with Note 3 on Property, Plant and Equipment.

nodes.title: Current income tax
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for income taxes, covering both current and deferred tax. Current income tax, including Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT), is measured per the Income-Tax Act, 1961, with rates enacted at the reporting date; items recognized outside profit or loss are recognized in OCI or equity, and management evaluates uncertain tax positions. Deferred tax uses the balance sheet approach for temporary differences, with exceptions for initial recognition of goodwill or certain transactions, and for investments in subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures where reversal timing is controlled or not probable. Deferred tax assets are recognized for deductible temporary differences and unused tax credits/losses when probable taxable profit exists, subject to similar exceptions, and are reviewed at each reporting date. Measurement uses expected enacted tax rates, and deferred tax on outside-profit-or-loss items is recognized accordingly. MAT credit is recognized as an asset when sufficient taxable temporary differences or convincing evidence exist, reviewed and written down if necessary, and included in deferred tax.

nodes.title: Deferred tax
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies from the Notes to the Standalone Financial Statements for the year ended March 31, 2025, of Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited. It details deferred tax accounting, including recognition and measurement of deferred tax assets and liabilities, exceptions, review, and MAT credit. It also covers Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE) policy, including cost, depreciation methods, useful lives, capitalization of borrowing costs, revaluation, derecognition, and transfer of assets under concession agreements. Additionally, it outlines intangible assets policy, covering recognition, amortization, useful lives, and impairment.

nodes.title: i) Right-of-Use Assets
nodes.summary: The text outlines the accounting policy for right-of-use assets, covering initial recognition at lease commencement, measurement at cost including lease liabilities, initial direct costs, and lease payments less incentives, subsequent measurement involving depreciation on a straight-line basis over the shorter of lease term or useful life, depreciation using useful life if ownership transfers or a purchase option is exercised, adjustment for remeasurement of lease liabilities, and subjection to impairment per section (m).

nodes.title: ii) Lease Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text outlines lease liability accounting: initial measurement at present value of lease payments, including fixed, variable (index/rate-based), residual guarantees, purchase options, and termination penalties; excludes non-indexed variable payments (expensed when incurred). Present value uses incremental borrowing rate if implicit rate is indeterminable. Subsequently, liabilities increase with interest accretion and decrease with payments, and are remeasured for modifications, lease term or payment changes, or purchase option reassessment.

nodes.title: iii) Short-term leases and leases of low-value assets
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: short-term and low-value lease exemptions, with expenses on a straight-line basis; lessor accounting for long-term leases, distinguishing finance and operating leases, and income recognition for cancellable and non-cancellable leases; inventory valuation at lower of cost and net realizable value, including stores and spares; impairment of non-financial assets, including recoverable amount determination, value in use, fair value less costs of disposal, reversal of impairment, and annual testing of goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles; provisions, contingent liabilities, and contingent assets, including recognition, measurement, and discounting; operational claim provisions; retirement and employee benefits, covering provident fund, gratuity, and accumulated leave; and an introduction to financial instruments.

nodes.title: Initial recognition and measurement
nodes.summary: The text outlines initial recognition and measurement of financial assets at fair value plus transaction costs (unless at FVTPL), with trade receivables without significant financing component at transaction price. It details subsequent measurement categories: debt instruments at amortised cost (held to collect SPPI cash flows, using effective interest rate method, with impairment in P&L), debt instruments at FVTPL (residual category, held for trading, fair value changes in P&L), debt instruments at FVTOCI (held to collect and sell SPPI cash flows), and equity investments (measured at fair value, with irrevocable FVTOCI election for fair value changes in OCI without recycling, or FVTPL with changes in P&L).

nodes.title: Subsequent Measurement of Financial Assets: Amortised Cost, FVTPL, FVTOCI
nodes.summary: The page explains subsequent measurement of financial assets, classifying debt instruments into three categories: amortised cost, fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL), and fair value through other comprehensive income (FVTOCI). For amortised cost, it details the two conditions: business model to hold assets for collecting contractual cash flows and solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI), noting this category is most relevant to the Company, measured using the effective interest rate (EIR) method with impairment losses in profit or loss. FVTPL is a residual category for debt instruments not meeting amortised cost or FVTOCI criteria, measured at fair value with changes in profit or loss, including held-for-trading assets. FVTOCI applies when the business model collects contractual cash flows and sells financial assets, with SPPI terms.

nodes.title: Equity investments
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies under Ind AS: equity investments measured at fair value with irrevocable FVTOCI or FVTPL election; FVTOCI changes in OCI without recycling but transferable within equity; FVTPL changes in P&L. Subsidiaries and joint ventures at cost less impairment. Perpetual debt classified as equity under Ind AS 32. Derecognition criteria based on expiry of cash flow rights or transfer of risks, rewards, and control, including continuing involvement and guarantees. Impairment using ECL model for debt instruments at amortized cost or FVTOCI, lease receivables, and trade receivables, with simplified approach for trade and lease receivables recognizing lifetime ECL, and significant increase in credit risk assessment for other assets.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Perpetual Debt and Derecognition of Financial Assets
nodes.summary: The page outlines accounting policies for investments in subsidiaries and joint ventures at cost less impairment, then covers perpetual debt and derecognition. Perpetual debt is a subordinated instrument redeemable at issuer's option with a fixed coupon deferrable if dividends are unpaid, classified as equity under Ind AS 32. Derecognition of financial assets occurs when cash flow rights expire or are transferred under a pass-through arrangement with risks/rewards or control transferred. If neither transferred nor retained substantially all risks and rewards nor control, the company recognizes the asset to the extent of continuing involvement and an associated liability, measured to reflect retained rights and obligations. Guarantees are measured at the lower of original carrying amount and maximum repayment consideration.

nodes.title: Impairment of financial assets
nodes.summary: The text details the impairment of financial assets using the expected credit loss (ECL) model for debt instruments at amortised cost or FVTOCI, lease receivables under Ind AS 116, and trade receivables under Ind AS 115. It describes the simplified approach for trade and lease receivables, recognizing lifetime ECLs without tracking credit risk changes, and the general approach for other assets based on significant credit risk increases, using 12-month or lifetime ECLs. ECL is defined as the difference between contractual and expected cash flows discounted at the original EIR, recognized in P&L. Balance sheet presentation as an allowance and grouping by shared credit risk characteristics are covered. It also addresses financial liabilities: initial classification and measurement at fair value, subsequent measurement categories including FVTPL, recognition of gains/losses, and treatment of own credit risk for designated FVTPL liabilities.

nodes.title: Financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for financial instruments under Ind AS 109. It covers Expected Credit Loss (ECL) impairment, distinguishing between 12-month and lifetime ECL based on significant increases in credit risk, and describes ECL measurement, recognition in P&L, and balance sheet presentation as an allowance. It details grouping of instruments by shared credit risk characteristics. For financial liabilities, it covers initial recognition and classification (FVTPL, loans and borrowings, payables, derivatives), subsequent measurement (FVTPL with gains/losses in P&L, and amortised cost using EIR), financial guarantee contracts (initial FVTPL, subsequent higher of loss allowance or initial amount less cumulative income), derecognition, reclassification of financial assets (only for debt instruments upon business model change, prospective application), and offsetting of financial instruments.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies for Loans, Guarantees, Derecognition, and Reclassification
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for loans and borrowings, financial guarantee contracts, derecognition of financial liabilities, and reclassification of financial assets. Loans and borrowings are measured at amortised cost using the effective interest rate (EIR) method, with gains/losses recognized in profit or loss. Financial guarantee contracts are initially recognized at fair value through profit or loss, then measured at the higher of loss allowance or initially recognized amount less cumulative income. Derecognition occurs when obligations are discharged, cancelled, or expire, or when terms are substantially modified. Reclassification of financial assets is only for debt instruments upon a change in business model, applied prospectively from the reclassification date, with no restatement of prior gains, losses, or interest.

nodes.title: Offsetting of financial instruments
nodes.summary:
Offsetting of financial instruments
Financial assets and financial liabilities are offset and the net amount is reported in the balance sheet if there is a currently enforceable legal right to offset the recognised amounts and there is an intention to settle on a net basis, to realise the assets and settle the liabilities simultaneously.

nodes.title: Initial recognition and subsequent measurement
nodes.summary: The text covers initial recognition and subsequent measurement of derivative financial instruments (forward contracts, swaps, options, futures) at fair value through profit or loss, with gains/losses in profit and loss. It also covers redeemable preference shares recognized at fair value as financial liabilities, with liability and equity components allocated and transaction costs apportioned. Cash and cash equivalents include cash, bank balances, and short-term deposits with insignificant risk. Cash dividends are recognized as liabilities when authorized and no longer at the Company's discretion, with a corresponding equity entry. Earnings per share includes basic and diluted calculations. Business combinations are accounted using the acquisition method under Ind AS 103, with cost measured at fair value of assets transferred, equity instruments issued, and liabilities incurred.

nodes.title: Redeemable preference shares

It details derivative financial instruments (recognition, measurement, and gains/losses), redeemable preference shares (liability and equity components), cash and cash equivalents, cash dividend recognition, and earnings per share (basic and diluted). It also covers business combinations using the acquisition and pooling of interests methods, including goodwill and provisional amounts, and amended standards adopted (Ind AS 117 and amendments to other Ind AS, and Ind AS 116 lease liability amendments). Finally, it addresses significant accounting judgements, estimates, and assumptions.

nodes.title: (A) Judgements
nodes.summary: The text describes management's significant judgements in applying accounting policies, specifically regarding de facto control over entities where the Company holds less than a majority voting rights. It details three cases: (i) Dholera Infrastructure Private Limited (49% ownership, control via shareholder agreement), (ii) Mundra Solar Technopark Private Limited (49% ownership, control via business takeover and shareholder agreement), and (iii) Mundra LPG Terminal Private Limited (48.97% ownership, control via additional investment and management/operational control from April 2022). All are treated as subsidiaries due to practical ability to direct relevant activities.

nodes.title: (B) Estimates and assumptions
nodes.summary: The text covers key accounting estimates and assumptions: impairment of financial assets (based on default risk and expected cash loss, using historical and market data), taxes (deferred tax assets recognition based on probable future taxable profits and tax planning), fair value measurement (using market observable data or third-party valuers with judgment on liquidity, credit, and volatility risks), and depreciation/amortization (reviewing useful lives and residual values annually). It then presents Note 3 on Property, Plant and Equipment, detailing cost, accumulated depreciation, additions, deductions, and net block for various asset classes for FY 2024 and 2025, including disclosures on water pipeline, leasehold land development, reclaimed land pending registration, operating lease land, project assets, and security charges.

nodes.summary: The text presents quantitative fair value hierarchy disclosures for financial assets and liabilities as of March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024, with tables showing Level 1, 2, and 3 inputs. Assets include unquoted equity at FVTOCI, government and trust securities, and derivatives; liabilities include derivatives. Derivative valuation uses observable inputs like yield curves and FX rates; government securities use quoted prices. A call option agreement on equity investment has nil fair value, valued via Black-Scholes with inputs: volatility 38%, risk-free rate 5.60%, intrinsic value nil. It describes significant unobservable inputs for Level 3 measurements using Cost Approach (Summation Method) with underlying assets as input and sensitivity analysis. It notes a change from DCF to Cost Approach for unquoted equity FVTOCI assets based on a registered valuer's report.

nodes.title: c) Financial Instrument measured at Amortised Cost
nodes.summary: The section covers financial instruments measured at amortised cost, with carrying amounts approximating fair values. It details financial risk management objectives and policies, including market, credit, liquidity, and equity price risks, overseen by senior management and the Central Treasury Team under a Board-approved policy. Derivative instruments used for hedging include cross currency swaps, interest rate swaps, options, and forwards, with no speculative trading. Market risk includes interest rate, foreign currency, and equity price risks, with sensitivity analyses. Credit risk covers trade receivables, financing activities, and concentration risk. Liquidity risk addresses maturity mismatches and undiscounted cash flows. Capital management objectives and gearing ratio calculations are provided. Capital commitments, other commitments (pledged shareholding and letters of support), and contingent liabilities are disclosed. Significant interests in subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures are listed, along with details of funds loaned to intermediaries and statutory disclosures, including post-balance sheet events such as the Abbot Point Port acquisition and dividend recommendation.

nodes.title: 34.3 Financial Risk Management objective and policies
nodes.summary: The text covers the amortised cost measurement of financial instruments, noting carrying amounts approximate fair values. It details financial risk management objectives and policies, listing principal financial liabilities (loans, borrowings, payables, lease liabilities, guarantees) and assets (loans, investments, receivables, cash). It identifies market, credit, liquidity, and equity price risks, and describes oversight by senior management and the Central Treasury Team under a Board-approved policy. Derivative instruments used for hedging include cross currency swaps, interest rate swaps, options, and forwards, with no speculative trading. It addresses counterparty credit risk, daily mark-to-market monitoring, and recognition of gains/losses in profit and loss.

nodes.title: a) Market risk
nodes.summary: The text defines market risk as the risk that fair value of future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate due to changes in market prices. It identifies three types: interest rate risk, currency risk, and other price risk such as equity price risk. Financial instruments affected include loans and borrowings, deposits, FVTOCI investments, short term investments, and derivative financial instruments. It states that sensitivity analysis relates to positions as at March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2024, prepared on the basis that net debt, the ratio of fixed to floating interest rates of debt and derivatives, and the proportion of financial instruments in foreign currencies remain constant. The analysis excludes impacts on carrying values of gratuity and other post-retirement obligations and provisions. It also lists assumptions: sensitivity of relevant profit or loss item is the effect of assumed changes in respective market risks, based on financial assets and liabilities held at those dates.

nodes.title: (i) Interest rate risk
nodes.summary: The text discusses the Company's interest rate risk, including its exposure from financing, investing, and cash management, primarily related to long-term debt with floating interest rates. It outlines management strategies such as maintaining a balanced portfolio of fixed and variable rate loans and using interest rate swaps or futures. It also presents an interest rate sensitivity analysis, showing that a 50 basis point increase/decrease would decrease/increase profit before tax by ₹10.07 crore (previous year ₹5.55 crore), based on year-end risk exposure, and notes that year-end balances may not represent average debt.

nodes.title: (ii) Foreign currency risk
nodes.summary: The text covers three financial risk types. Foreign currency risk discusses exposure to USD, EUR, CHF, SGD, and CNY, hedging via swaps, forwards, and natural hedges, with sensitivity analysis showing profit and equity impacts for 1% rate changes. Equity price risk covers non-listed securities, diversification, pledged investments, and corporate guarantees. Credit risk includes trade receivables and financing activities, customer credit assessment, impairment analysis, bank and counterparty limits, corporate guarantees of ₹9,406.14 crore, and concentration risk from Mundra customers (62% revenue, 42% receivables). Liquidity risk is defined as difficulty meeting financial commitments.

nodes.title: Equity Price Risk and Credit Risk Disclosures in Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The page covers equity price risk and credit risk disclosures. Equity price risk section discusses non-listed equity securities' susceptibility to market price risk, management through diversification and limits, regular reporting to senior management, Board approval of investment decisions, and corporate guarantees and pledged equity for collateral. Credit risk section defines credit risk, exposure from operating and financing activities, customer credit risk management policies, impairment analysis at reporting date for major and minor receivables, treasury management for bank balances and counterparty limits, corporate guarantees given to banks for subsidiaries and joint ventures amounting to ₹9,406.14 crore (previous year ₹8,301.34 crore), and concentration of credit risk due to dependence on customers at Mundra, including revenue percentage and receivables concentration.

nodes.title: c) Liquidity risk
nodes.summary: The text defines liquidity risk as the risk of difficulty in raising funds to meet commitments tied to financial instruments settled in cash or another financial asset, and the risk of being unable to sell a financial asset quickly near fair value. It outlines the Company's liquidity risk management framework for short, medium, and long-term funding, noting exposure arises from maturity mismatches between financial assets and liabilities. The Company manages this by maintaining adequate cash and cash equivalents and having bank credit facilities for timely, cost-effective coverage of operating commitments. It presents tables analyzing derivative and non-derivative financial liabilities into maturity groupings (less than 1 year, 1–5 years, over 5 years) based on remaining contractual maturity, showing contractual undiscounted cash flows for borrowings, interest on borrowings, trade payables, lease liabilities (including finance charge), and other financial liabilities, with totals and carrying values, for March 31, 2025 and 2024. Notes clarify the table is based on undiscounted contractual maturities including interest, ignores refinancing options, variable interest amounts may change, and foreign currency liabilities are converted to INR at the reporting date exchange rate.

nodes.title: 34.4 Capital management
nodes.summary: The text covers the company's capital management objectives, including maximizing shareholder value, managing capital structure, and monitoring gearing ratio. It provides a table showing gearing ratio calculations for March 31, 2025, and 2024, with components like total borrowings, cash and bank balance, net debt, total equity, and gearing ratio percentages. It notes compliance with financial covenants and no changes in capital management objectives. Additionally, it includes information required under the MSMED Act, detailing principal and interest amounts due to suppliers, interest paid, and accrued interest for the years ended March 31, 2025, and 2024.

Finally, it notes the Board’s responsibility for overseeing the financial reporting process.

nodes.title: Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary:
Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Consolidated Financial Statements
Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the consolidated financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor’s report that includes our opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance, but is not a guarantee that an audit
conducted in accordance with Standards on Auditing (“SAs”) will always detect a material misstatement when it exists. Misstatements can arise from fraud or error and are considered material if, individually or in the aggregate, they could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of these consolidated financial statements.
We give in “Annexure A” a detailed description of Auditor’s responsibilities for Audit of the consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Consolidation procedure:
nodes.summary: The section covers consolidation procedures including combining parent and subsidiary items, eliminating investments and intragroup transactions, attributing profit/OCI to parent and non-controlling interests, accounting for changes in ownership or loss of control, and applying the equity method for associates and joint ventures. It also addresses current versus non-current classification of assets and liabilities, foreign currency transactions and translation, fair value measurement including hierarchy and valuation techniques, revenue recognition across various operations and service concession arrangements, government grants, exceptional items, and taxes. Additionally, it outlines accounting policies for property, plant and equipment, intangible assets, investment properties, borrowing costs, leases, inventories, impairment, provisions, employee benefits, financial instruments, derivatives, hedge accounting, redeemable preference shares, cash and cash equivalents, dividends, goodwill, business combinations, non-current assets held for sale, and earnings per share, along with new standards adopted and significant judgements and estimates.

nodes.title: a) Investment in associates and joint venture entities
nodes.summary: The text details consolidation procedures: combining parent and subsidiary items, eliminating investments and intragroup transactions, attributing profit/OCI to parent and non-controlling interests, and accounting for changes in ownership or loss of control. It also covers accounting for associates and joint ventures using the equity method, including initial recognition, adjustments for share of net assets, treatment of transaction costs, recognition of share of profits/losses and OCI, elimination of unrealized gains/losses, impairment assessment, and derecognition upon loss of significant influence or joint control.

nodes.title: b) Current versus non-current classification

It specifies that deferred tax assets and liabilities are non-current and defines the operating cycle as twelve months. Additionally, it covers foreign currency transactions, including functional currency determination, initial and subsequent measurement using spot rates, translation of foreign operations for consolidation at reporting date rates with average rates for income and expenses, and recognition of exchange differences in OCI as Foreign Currency Translation Reserve, reclassified to profit or loss on disposal.

nodes.title: d) Fair value measurement

Management's role in determining policies and procedures for recurring and non-recurring measurements is described, along with external valuers' involvement, selection criteria, and annual decisions. The note details the process for analyzing fair value movements, verifying inputs against contracts, and comparing changes with external sources. It also references related disclosures on valuation methods, estimates, hierarchy, unquoted equity shares, and financial instruments, and describes determining classes of assets and liabilities for disclosure purposes.

nodes.title: d) Details of Equity Shares held by Promoter & Promotor Group at the end of the year
nodes.summary: This section provides detailed shareholding information for Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited's Promoter and Promoter Group as of March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024. It lists equity shares held by 13 promoters/entities, totaling 1,42,33,76,085 shares (65.89%), including individual, trust, and corporate holdings with percentage changes. It also details non-cumulative redeemable preference shares held by two trusts (Priti G. Adani and Shilin R. Adani on behalf of S.B. Adani Family Trust), totaling 25,01,824 shares (100%). Additionally, it covers other equity components such as the equity component of preference shares, securities premium, reserves (general, debenture redemption, capital redemption, tonnage tax), retained earnings, and capital reserve, with opening/closing balances and changes. It further includes Other Comprehensive Income items: Foreign Currency Translation Reserve, Cash Flow Hedge Reserve, and Equity Instruments through OCI, along with notes on exchange differences, hedge recycling, and revaluation. Finally, it addresses dividend distribution (cash dividends on equity and preference shares) and compliance with the Companies Act, 2013.

nodes.title: Promoter and Promoter Group Name
nodes.summary: The text presents shareholding details for Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited's Promoter and Promoter Group as of March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024. It lists equity shares held by 13 promoters/entities, including individual holdings, trust holdings, and corporate entities, with the number of shares, percentage of total shares, and percentage change during the year. The total equity shares held are 1,42,33,76,085 (65.89%). It also details non-cumulative redeemable preference shares held by two trusts (Priti G. Adani and Shilin R. Adani on behalf of S.B. Adani Family Trust) as of both dates, including number of shares and percentage of total. The text is part of notes to consolidated financial statements (Share Capital) in the Integrated Annual Report 2024-25.

nodes.title: Promoter Shareholding in Equity and Preference Shares
nodes.summary: The page presents shareholding details of the Promoter and Promoter Group of Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited as of March 31, 2024, and March 31, 2025. It lists the names of promoter entities and individuals, the number of equity shares held at year-end, the percentage change during the year, and the percentage of total shares for each holder, totaling 1,42,33,76,085 equity shares (65.89% of total shares). It also provides details of non-cumulative redeemable preference shares held by Priti G. Adani and Shilin R. Adani (on behalf of S.B. Adani Family Trust) for both years, showing shares held, percentage change, and percentage of total preference shares, totaling 25,01,824 shares (100%).

nodes.title: Promoter and Promoter Group Name
nodes.summary: The text presents notes to the consolidated financial statements of Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited for the year ended March 31, 2025. It details share capital, including promoter and promoter group holdings of equity shares and non-cumulative redeemable preference shares, with number of shares, percentage of total shares, and changes during the year. It then covers other equity components: equity component of non-cumulative redeemable preference shares, securities premium, general reserve, debenture redemption reserve, capital redemption reserve, tonnage tax reserve, retained earnings, and capital reserve. For each, opening balance, changes, closing balance, and explanatory notes are provided.

nodes.title: Other Comprehensive Income
key_items: Particulars Cash Flow Hedge Reserve (refer note 34.3(A)(ii))

nodes.summary: The text presents Other Comprehensive Income components for Adani Ports and SEZ: Foreign Currency Translation Reserve, showing opening, changes, and closing balances; Cash Flow Hedge Reserve, detailing effective losses, recycling, and joint venture share; and Equity Instrument through OCI, with fair value changes. It includes notes on recognition of exchange differences, hedge reserve reclassification, and revaluation gains/losses. It also covers total other equity, dividend distribution made and proposed—cash dividends on equity and preference shares, per-share amounts, and compliance with the Companies Act, 2013 regarding proposed dividends.

structure.title: 14 Non-Current Borrowings
structure.summary: Note 14 details non-current borrowings as of March 31, 2025, with comparative 2024 figures. It lists secured non-convertible redeemable debentures with interest rates, redemption schedules, and security (Mundra Port assets, subsidiary assets). It includes foreign currency bonds with coupon rates and US Treasury spreads, the liability component of preference shares, and secured/unsecured foreign currency and rupee loans from banks and others. It also covers foreign currency letters of credit, trade credits, and subsidiary borrowings (debentures, term loans, related-party loans, supplier bills) with their security and repayment terms. Reconciliations of secured/unsecured amounts and current portions are provided.

nodes.title: Debentures
nodes.summary: Note 14, Non-Current Borrowings, lists three series of secured Non-Convertible Redeemable Debentures: 15,000 8.50% debentures (redeemable April 12, 2030), 2,520 9.35% debentures (redeemable July 04, 2026), and 16,000 7.65% debentures (redeemable in three installments in October 2025, 2026, and 2027). The table presents amounts in crore for both non-current and current portions as of March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2024, showing corresponding previous-year figures for each category.

nodes.title: Particulars
nodes.summary: This note details non-current borrowings as of March 31, 2025, including various secured non-convertible redeemable debentures with differing interest rates, face values, and redemption schedules, along with comparative figures. It also lists foreign currency bonds priced at spreads over US Treasury Notes, the liability component of preference shares, and foreign currency loans from banks and others, both secured and unsecured. The information is presented in crores, showing non-current and current portions for the current and previous years.

nodes.title: Non-Current Borrowings: Foreign Currency Bonds and Preference Shares
nodes.summary: The text presents details of non-current borrowings from Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited's consolidated financial statements for FY2024-25. It lists seven foreign currency bonds, each with coupon rates (5%, 3.828%, 3.10%, 4.375%, 4.20%, 4%, 3.375%) and pricing over respective US Treasury Notes (ranging from 150 to 376 basis points over 5 to 20 years), all unsecured, with cross-references to notes f(i) through f(vii). Additionally, it covers the liability component of 0.01% non-cumulative redeemable preference shares (unsecured), referencing note 12(b).

nodes.title: Foreign currency loans
nodes.summary: The text presents a financial table detailing non-current and current portions of foreign currency and rupee loans from banks and others (secured and unsecured), along with foreign currency letters of credit, as of March 31, 2025 and 2024. It includes amounts in crore, references to notes, and a breakdown of secured/unsecured borrowings. Additionally, notes describe secured non-convertible redeemable debentures, specifying amounts and the assets (e.g., Mundra Port terminals) on which they are secured.

nodes.title: Non-Current Borrowings: Portfolio Overview and Secured Debentures
nodes.summary: The page presents Note 14 on Non-Current Borrowings as of March 31, 2025, with comparative figures for 2024. It details non-current and current portions of Rupee Loans from banks and other financial institutions (secured and unsecured), Foreign currency letters of credit from banks (secured and unsecured), and amounts from others. It includes a reconciliation of secured and unsecured borrowings and amounts disclosed under current borrowings. Notes describe specific secured Non-Convertible Redeemable Debentures, detailing their amounts and the assets securing them, including project assets at Mundra Port and those of a wholly owned subsidiary.

nodes.title: Notes:
nodes.summary: This note on non-current borrowings presents a detailed table of secured and unsecured loans from banks, financial institutions, and others, including rupee loans and foreign currency letters of credit, split into non-current and current portions for March 31, 2025 and 2024. It discloses secured and unsecured borrowing totals and amounts classified as current borrowings. Notes describe secured non-convertible redeemable debentures backed by charges on Mundra Port terminal assets and subsidiary assets, including redemptions during the year. It also details foreign currency bonds with amounts, interest rates, and bullet repayment years, a prepaid bond, secured trade credits, and various rupee and foreign currency term loans with interest rates and repayment schedules.

nodes.title: g) Loans taken by the subsidiaries includes:
nodes.summary: This note details borrowings of various subsidiaries, including secured non-convertible redeemable debentures (Ocean Sparkle) with mortgage of marine assets and quarterly repayments; foreign currency term loans from banks (Shanti Sagar, Mediterranean International Ports, Adani International Ports Holdings) secured by asset charges, share pledges, and repayable in installments or bullet; loans by Adani Agri Logistics secured by project assets; loans from related parties (Adinath Polyfills); supplier bills under foreign letters of credit (Adani Harbour Services, Adani Vizhinjam Port) with interest rates and maturities; trade credit facilities (Adani Gangavaram Port) some repaid; letters of credit for equipment or logistics (Adani Forwarding Agent, Adani Logistics, Adani Krishnapatnam Port); rupee term loans (Gopalpur Ports, Karaikal Port) secured by mortgages; foreign currency term loan (East Africa Gateway); unsecured loans and secured vessel/term loans (Astro Offshore); repaid rupee term loans (Adani Agri Logistics entities); unsecured letter of credit (HM Agri Logistics); and foreign currency letters of credit/trade credits (BU Agri Logistics).
